newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zairean rebels advance on refugee camps.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels advance on refugee camps.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Saturday his forces were advancing on three fronts and closing in on refugee camps he says are the bastion of Rwanda's former Hutu army.

Speaking to Reuters in the rebel capital Goma, Kabila said his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) had opened up humanitarian routes for the more than 100,000 Rwandan refugees.

But Kabila, whose forces are engaging Zaire's ragged army, mercenaries and Rwanda's ousted Hutu army on several fronts, said the refugees were being used as cannon fodder by the Zaireans and their allies.
Kabila said his forces were 19 km (12 miles) outside the Tingi-Tingi refugee camp and there was fighting in Punia, about 70 km (45 miles) south of Lubutu.

The head of the U.N. refugee agency, Sadako Ogata, flew to the main government-held eastern town of Kisangani on Saturday. But it was unclear if her planned visit to Tingi-Tingi would go ahead. The World Food Programme (WFP) said in a statement on Saturday some of its top staff flew to Tingi-Tingi on Friday and found the refugees in a precarious condition.
"Our forces have opened up a humanitarian corridor to allow the refugees to go back home but these people are being held against their will," Kabila said.

He said the refugees, who fled Rwanda in 1994 after many of them took part in genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus, were being pushed further into the bush and towards Kisangani by the Zaireans.

"The United Nations must come out in the open and condemn the Zairean army for not allowing these people back to Rwanda. Paying visits to the refugees will not solve the problem," Kabila said in reference to Ogata's planned visit.
Kabila reported more battlefield victories on Saturday after rejecting international mediation in the conflict with ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Kabila said there was fighting in the tin and gold mining town of Punia. Defence officials in Kinshasa said on Friday that Punia, on the road to Kisangani, was in danger of falling.

The rebel leader said his forces continued to besiege the airfield and army base at Kindu, one of two bases for Kinshasa's counter-offensive, saying his forces expected to take Kindu in the next few days.

Kabila's Alliance has steadily eroded Mobutu's control in eastern Zaire since the rebellion began last October. The Alliance now claims to control a narrow border strip about 1,400 km (875 miles) long.
Mobutu returned home on Friday after medical tests for his prostate cancer in Europe and a three-day working visit to Morocco, a longtime ally.
Leaving after talks with King Hassan, Mobutu denied he had asked for Moroccan troops and materiel to combat the rebels, accused by Zaire of being the puppets of Rwanda and Uganda.
But Kabila claimed to know Hassan had turned down Mobutu's request for troops and thanked the Moroccan monarch.
Kabila, who believes the end of Mobutu's 32-year rule is approaching, on Friday rejected international mediation to end Africa's latest war. He said the war must be resolved by the Zaireans.

He was responding to calls from several African nations for international mediation in the war sparked off by Zairean attempts to expel the Banyamulenge -- an ethnic Tutsi group -- back to Rwanda, a land they left up to 200 years ago.
The Banyamulenge took up arms to resist the expulsions and joined Kabila, a veteran opposition figure against Mobutu.
Kabila said he was only willing to meet Mobutu on a one-to-one basis to discuss Mobutu's handover of power.
